comparator.name: University College Venlo (Sustainable Food Systems, Liberal Arts and Sciences)
comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027 (Education and Examination Regulations 2026-2027, Maastricht School of Liberal Arts and Sciences, UCV programme, in force 1 September 2026, and UCV Course Catalogue 2026-2027; programme pages checked 2026-10-03)
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme pages (s2, s3, s4) describe the curriculum in words only: eight core courses on the biology of nutrition, behaviour and decision-making, the philosophy of science and global sustainability challenges, elective courses organised around three pillars (Behaviour, Health, Responsible Innovation) that a student may specialise in or combine, skills trainings, two project periods per year and a one-semester Capstone. They give no EC for the whole programme, so the 180-EC reconstruction uses the 2026-2027 Education and Examination Regulations of the Maastricht School of Liberal Arts and Sciences (s0, UCV programme): Article 3.6 (180 EC), 3.8 (core of four 5-EC courses; general education of 2-4 courses and 10-20 EC outside the concentration, with at least one humanities course), 3.9 (concentration of 14-16 courses and 70-80 EC with at least 20 EC advanced; five skills trainings of 12.5 EC; three projects of 15 EC; a 20-EC Capstone) and Appendix I, together with the UCV Course Catalogue 2026-2027 (s1), which gives 5 EC to every course and project, 2.5 EC to every skills training and 20 EC to the Capstone. The new core applies to students starting in September 2026: VCO1006, VCO1007, VCO1002 and VCO1008 (20 EC), the core projects VPR1006 and VPR1002 (10 EC) and the core skills trainings VSK1001, VSK1002, VSK1000 and VSK1004 (10 EC); the catalogue also lists VSK3000 Portfolio (2.5 EC) as a core skills training. Article 3.8(1) states a combined 20 EC for core skills trainings and projects whereas the Appendix items sum to 22.5 EC; the reconstruction counts every Appendix item, which makes the fixed components total 90 EC (core courses 20, core projects 10, core skills 12.5, concentration skills 12.5, concentration projects 15, Capstone 20). The remaining 90 EC are general education and concentration courses; the regulations allow 10-20 and 70-80 EC, and the instantiation is the midpoint (3 general-education courses, 15 EC; 15 concentration courses, 75 EC), which is valid. Which pillar a student specialises in, the elective courses, the general-education courses, the choice of skills trainings and projects and the Capstone topic are individual choices that the sources do not fix, so they are kept as explicit restricted-choice components without invented course names, and no formal route is selected because the pillars are an optional orientation rather than formal routes. Checked 2026-10-03. A human may wish to confirm the 20 versus 22.5 EC treatment of the core skills and projects in Article 3.8(1) and Appendix I.

General education: three courses outside the concentration (restricted choice, 10-20 EC range; at least one humanities course and one course in the alternate perspective)
Concentration courses: fifteen courses addressing food-system challenges through behaviour, health and/or responsible innovation (restricted choice, 14-16 courses and 70-80 EC range)
Concentration skills trainings: five at intermediate or advanced level (restricted choice)
Concentration projects: three, at least one advanced (restricted choice)

core: Academic core: the four core courses on the biology of nutrition and health, behaviour and decision-making, knowledge, evidence and decision-making under uncertainty (philosophy of science), and global sustainability challenges, with the Food in Transition systems project

Research methods, statistics and applied research training: designing quantitative and qualitative research, the Applied Researcher project sequence with statistical analysis, data visualisation, laboratory skills and science communication
Sustainable food systems and their environmental dimension: sustainable agriculture and food production, the environmental impact of food and global sustainability challenges
Cross-pillar integration: building a curriculum across the behaviour, health and responsible-innovation pillars to connect disciplines in the food system
Advanced concentration depth: at least 20 EC of advanced courses over no fewer than three courses, an advanced project and the 20-EC Capstone
adjacent: Health pillar: how nutrition affects the body and society, covering nutrition, metabolism, physiology, disease mechanisms, pharmacology and public health
Behaviour pillar: why people do what they do around food, covering consumer behaviour, decision-making, the psychology of eating, behaviour change and sensory perception
Responsible-innovation pillar: how knowledge becomes real change, covering entrepreneurship, product innovation, markets and economics, governance, regulation and policy
questions: Why do people eat unhealthily even when they know better, and how can food choices and health behaviour be changed?
How can sustainable food innovations reach the market and how can regulation steer food systems towards health and sustainability?
How do food production and consumption affect the environment and climate, and what must be done about it?

has teams design and develop a consumer product in a simulated industrial design-and-development environment, with customer interviews, modelling and prototyping; it makes a specific complementary contribution to product development in the responsible-innovation pillar, without any food content

covers social cognition, attitudes, groups and social influence on behaviour; it directly implements the psychological foundation of the behaviour pillar

introduces supply and demand, consumer behaviour theory, the theory of the firm, market structure and macroeconomic markets; it directly implements the economics of food markets at introductory level, without food-specific content

alternatives.label: Closest match to University College Venlo: Food, Behaviour and Health Systems with Sustainability and Innovation
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has four courses in biology, human physiology and public health, five in psychology, behavioural economics, consumer behaviour and communication, six in sustainability, ecology, governance and applied sustainability research (including the only food-production course), five in entrepreneurship, product design, economics and international governance, three in research methods, data and evidence, and Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore an interdisciplinary programme on behaviour, health, sustainability and innovation around food systems, but it contains no nutrition-science, food-technology or food-safety course, so the label names the field as food systems studied through these perspectives and not as a food-science programme.
alternatives.concept: UCV has no single elective curriculum: every student takes the same core on the biology of nutrition and health, behaviour and decision-making, the philosophy of science and global sustainability, plus a systems project and an applied-research line, and then builds the rest across the three pillars of behaviour, health and responsible innovation, or within one of them. The strongest defensible UCR response reproduces that cross-pillar structure for sustainable food systems: UCR counterparts of the biological, behavioural, evidence and sustainability core, research methods and data skills, an applied research project, and elective depth drawn from all three pillars with sustainability and food production (the one UCR course on farming) as the shared context.
progression: Foundations are placed before the courses that build on them where the formal rules allow: the gateway course Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine in semester 1 precedes Human Physiology and Biochemistry; Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes Microeconomics & Behavior, Behavioral Economics and Marketing & Consumer Engagement; Introduction to Economics and Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations precede Public Economics and International Business & Governance; the research project and the advanced courses fall in the final three semesters. Climate Change, Epidemiology and Consumer Product Design are open to the first semester. The two courses available only in semester 4 (Sustainable Farming & Innovation, Calling Bullshit) cannot move earlier.

alternatives.label: Health Pillar: Human Biology, Disease and Public Health with Sustainability Context
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has ten biomedical and life-science courses (the life-and-health gateway, cell biology, physiology, biochemistry, anatomy, laboratory, pharmacology, immunity, pathology and disease mechanisms) plus epidemiology and public health, four psychology and cognitive-neuroscience courses on health and perception, four methods and data courses, three sustainability and governance courses and one communication course, plus Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore a human-biology and health programme with a sustainability and food context, not a nutrition or food-science programme, because UCR has no nutrition course.
alternatives.concept: UCV organises its elective curriculum around three pillars and lets a student specialise in one. The health pillar, defined as how nutrition affects the body and society, is a stable study direction in the programme's own material and its catalogue fills it with biochemistry, physiology, molecular biology, pharmacology, pathobiology, microbiology, brain and action, public health and epidemiology courses. This alternative takes that pillar as its organising logic instead of the cross-pillar integration of Alternative 1: a programme on how the body works, how it fails and how population health is studied, with climate change and sustainability governance as the environmental context of food and health.
progression: The gateway courses Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine and Introduction to Brain & Behavior and Epidemiology & Public Health open semester 1 and precede every dependent biomedical, cognitive and psychology course; Human Physiology and Biochemistry (semester 3) precede Pharmacology, Molecular Pathology & Genetics and Mechanisms of Disease; Research Methods & Statistics and Statistics & Experimental Methods come before the Advanced Research Seminar in the final semester.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 integrates the three UCV pillars around sustainable food systems and has only five health-science courses; Alternative 2 specialises in the health pillar. It keeps eleven courses from Alternative 1 (including Personal & Professional Development) and replaces thirteen of Alternative 1's courses with courses in cell biology, anatomy, the life-science laboratory, pharmacology, immunity, pathology, disease mechanisms, health psychology, neuroscience and lifespan psychology, dropping the economics, entrepreneurship, marketing and consumer courses. The two programmes differ by 13 courses (97.5 EC), above the 30 EC / 4-course floor, and the differing courses follow directly from the change of organising pillar.

alternatives.label: Behaviour Pillar: Psychology, Decision-Making and Consumer Behaviour with Sustainability Context
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has eight psychology and cognitive-science courses (social psychology, statistics, health psychology, development, perception, higher-order cognition, research synthesis and the brain-and-behaviour gateway), three economics courses, three consumer-research, marketing and entrepreneurship courses, four communication and sociology courses, three methods and evidence courses, one public-health course, one sustainability course and Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore a behaviour and decision-making programme with a sustainability context, and food enters only through its applications because UCR has no food-behaviour course.
alternatives.concept: Behaviour is one of the three structurally embedded pillars of UCV, which asks why people do what they do around food, and its stable study direction and direct programme interests centre on food choice, consumer decision-making, the psychology of eating and why people eat unhealthily. This alternative takes that pillar as its organising logic: a programme on how people perceive, decide and change their behaviour, drawing on psychology, behavioural economics, consumer research, sociology and communication, with the research methods needed to study behaviour and with climate change as the sustainability setting of consumption.
progression: The gateway courses Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, Introduction to Economics and Epidemiology & Public Health open the first three semesters and precede the dependent psychology, cognition, economics and market-research courses; Research Methods & Statistics comes before Microeconomics & Behavior, Behavioral Economics and Marketing & Consumer Engagement; Statistics & Experimental Methods precedes the Advanced Research Seminar, and the advanced psychology and cognition courses fall in semesters 5 and 6.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 integrates the three UCV pillars and gives half its courses to sustainability, ecology, governance, health biology and entrepreneurship; Alternative 3 specialises in the behaviour pillar. It keeps thirteen courses from Alternative 1 (several of them shared methods and behavioural-economics courses) and replaces eleven with courses in psychology, cognitive neuroscience, sociology, qualitative research, market research and climate communication, dropping the biology, farming, life-cycle, governance and product-design courses. Against Alternative 2 it shares twelve courses (mainly shared psychology gateways and methods courses) and differs by twelve courses (90 EC). Both pairs pass the 30 EC / 4-course floor, and the differing courses follow from the change of organising pillar, not from substitution.

Food policy and regulation for health and sustainability

selection.assessment: Three UCR alternatives are defensible and the maximum was reached. UCV combines three pillars (behaviour, health, responsible innovation) around sustainable food systems and lets students specialise in one or combine them, so the closest response (Alternative 1) reproduces the cross-pillar structure and the shared core: it owns the five generator-eligible rows on sustainable food systems, the journey from production to consumption, sustainable agriculture, the environmental impact of food and research methods for food-system challenges (6111, 6112, 6119, 6120, 6128). Alternative 2 specialises in the health pillar (stable direction 6117 and direct interest 6121) and Alternative 3 in the behaviour pillar (6113, 6116, 6126); Alternative 2 shares 11 courses and Alternative 3 shares 13 courses with Alternative 1 and they share 12 with each other, so every pair differs by at least 11 courses and passes the 30 EC / 4-course floor. The responsible-innovation pillar (6114, 6118, 6122, 6124, 6125) and food policy and regulation (6115, 6123) are coherent and feasible directions that were not needed once three alternatives were included (maximum-reached); Alternative 1 already carries the entrepreneurship, product-design, economics and governance courses of that pillar. Support-only rows (6127, 6129 to 6132) strengthened directions but generated none, and the search-only rows (6133 to 6145) generated no alternative. No UCR nutrition-science, food-technology, food-safety or food-product-development course exists, so none of the three programmes can reproduce UCV's specialist food courses.

blocks: Academic core, evidence and research training

Both develop academic inquiry skills: Academic Inquiry and Information Literacy trains selecting and evaluating scientific sources, and Personal & Professional Development likewise teaches students to select and critically analyse academic sources, formulate research questions and arguments and write and present academically; Personal & Professional Development additionally covers personal development and community engagement.

Both teach research design: formulating research questions, operationalizing variables, sampling and choosing measurement and design; Research Methods & Statistics adds descriptive and inferential statistics and does not include the concept-publication writing exercise.

Both address how scientific claims are distinguished from pseudoscience and misinformation and how evidence is evaluated; Calling Bullshit is a critical-thinking course and does not offer the systematic epistemology and philosophy of science, or the sustainability-specific evidence, of Knowledge, Evidence and Decision-Making under Uncertainty.

Both are team research projects on applied problems that end in data analysis and reporting; The Applied Researcher III is the last period of a three-period project with R analysis, a journal-style article and a poster conference, whereas Research in a Sustainable Delta is a single project on a sustainability problem set by an external partner.

Both train the analysis of research data with descriptive and inferential statistics; Statistics & Experimental Methods teaches multivariate models (regression, factor analysis, ANOVA/ANCOVA) at a higher level than The Applied Researcher II, which also covers data collection within a project and uses R.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: The Applied Researcher I is the first period of a supervised group research project that produces a research proposal on a problem set by a UM researcher; no UCR course is a comparable project-planning training, and the research-design content of the methods courses is already aligned with Designing Research.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Portfolio is a skills training in which students narrate their curriculum choices and plan their further development; UCR has no corresponding course, and Personal & Professional Development, which is a Year 1 course, is aligned with the academic-inquiry skills training instead.

Both cover basic cell processes, homeostasis, the function of organ systems including digestion, and energy metabolism in the human body; Human Physiology is a general physiology course and does not give the explicit macronutrient and nutrition focus of Biological Foundations of Nutrition and Health.

Both study how people decide, including cognitive biases and the interaction of psychological processes with economic incentives; Behavioral Economics is an advanced economics course and does not apply the concepts to food choice, health behaviour or sustainability as Behaviour and Decision-Making does.
Sustainability, food production and global challenges

Both address major global sustainability challenges and the links between production systems, society and environmental outcomes; Climate Change focuses on climate drivers, impacts and governance and does not cover the range of sustainability challenges or the measurement of sustainability.

Both analyse a product or problem across its whole chain of processes with environmental, social and health consequences; Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy uses quantitative life-cycle assessment and does not model behavioural, biological and institutional feedbacks in the food system as Food in Transition does.
Open concentration, general education and Capstone

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: general education is an individual restricted choice of two to four courses outside the student's concentration that the sources do not name; the UCR programmes distribute their courses across fields differently and no single course corresponds to it.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the fifteen concentration courses depend on the pillars the student chooses and are not named in the sources; the UCR courses of each alternative appear in the blocks above without being forced onto this open component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the five concentration skills trainings are individual choices (for example laboratory, communication, leadership, visualisation or motivational interviewing) that the sources do not name, and UCR has no scheduled skills-training modules.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the three concentration projects are individual choices (for example Think Tank, Academic Debate or Writing a Research Proposal) that the sources do not fix and that no UCR course corresponds to as a unit.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the 20-EC Capstone is an individual extensive research project or product in the final semester; UCR has no scheduled Capstone course, and the standardized optional independent research element is shown against this component.

notes.text: The Sustainable Food Systems programme at University College Venlo combines behaviour, health and responsible innovation around the food system, from production to consumption. At UCR, students can approach food and sustainability through fields such as psychology and behavioural economics, human biology and public health, sustainability science and entrepreneurship. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than reproducing a full food-systems curriculum.

Both programmes include substantial study of the biology of health, behaviour and decision-making, sustainability and research methods. The University College Venlo catalogue additionally includes specialist work in nutrition and metabolism, food technology and processing, food safety, sensory science and food product development. UCR students can instead combine its biomedical, psychology, economics, sustainability and entrepreneurship courses, but those food-specific components are not offered at the same level of depth.
